questions.q: Glycerol is recovered from spent lye in the soap industry by
questions.explain: Glycerol has a very high boiling point and decomposes near it; lowering the external pressure lets it boil at a lower, safe temperature.

questions.q: Nitration of phenol with dilute HNO₃ gives o- and p-nitrophenol, which are separated by steam distillation. Which isomer distils over, and why?
options: p-Nitrophenol, because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding
o-Nitrophenol, because of intramolecular hydrogen bonding
o-Nitrophenol, because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding
p-Nitrophenol, because its molecules are more symmetrical
questions.explain: In o-nitrophenol the –OH bonds to the neighbouring –NO₂ within the same molecule, so molecules do not associate and the compound is steam volatile. The para isomer is held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds and stays in the flask.

questions.q: Which method is best for separating chloroform (b.p. 334 K) from aniline (b.p. 457 K)?
questions.explain: The boiling points differ by more than 100 K, so simple distillation works: chloroform distils first and aniline is left behind. Fractional distillation is needed only when boiling points are close.

questions.q: In steam distillation of an aniline–water mixture, the mixture boils
options: Below 373 K, because the vapour pressures of aniline and water together equal atmospheric pressure
At the normal boiling point of aniline
Above 373 K, because dissolved aniline raises the boiling point of water
At exactly 373 K, because only water vaporises
questions.explain: The mixture boils when p(organic) + p(water) = atmospheric pressure; each partial pressure is below p, so boiling occurs below 373 K and far below aniline's own boiling point.
